Agent.text: The check passes. Recording what's still open, then wrapping up.

I decided that the music would come from your own music files plus some built-in demo songs. A full streaming library needs licensed music and servers, and this is the closest thing that works today. You can change this.

I built "Wavelet", an ad-free music app for your computer. It opens to a page where you create an account or sign in, with a "keep me signed in" option. Accounts are stored privately on this computer. Inside, it has the layout you'd expect from a big music service: a home page with mixes and albums, search with genre tiles, your library, Liked Songs, and playlists you can create, rename and delete. Right-click any song to like it, queue it or add it to a playlist. The bottom bar has play/pause, next/previous, shuffle, repeat, a seek bar and volume. On the account page you can change your name or password, sign out or delete the account. An "Ad-free" badge stays at the top, and nothing ever interrupts the music.

The app comes with 15 demo songs across five made-up artists. The app creates their music itself, so they play straight away. You can also add a folder of your own songs (MP3, FLAC, WAV, OGG or M4A). I tested that sound plays and that skipping ahead within a song works, that the account rules work, and that the final check passes.

The main difference from the real service is that there's no online catalog of famous songs: you get only the demo songs and your own files. The name, logo, colours and cover art are all original rather than copied. The covers are simple patterns, not real album art, and accounts stay on this computer instead of an online server.

A good next step would be to ask for a "lyrics" or "sleep timer" feature, or to say whether you have an online music source you'd like the app to connect to.
